results.title: USF opens $33 million College of Nursing building to tackle Florida shortage
results.description: ____________ Bottom line Key takeaway: USF’s new $33 million College of Nursing expansion will help train students as Florida confronts a projected shortage of nearly 20,000 registered nurses. Core challenge: Expanding Florida’s nursing workforce quickly enough to meet growing health care needs without sacrificing the quality of training. What’s next: USF will fill the new classrooms and simulation labs while working to add 500 nursing students by 2028 and move more graduates into Florida’s health care workforce. ____________ Nursing student Ariana Sawyer knows that one day, a patient will trust her with their life. That reality can be intimidating. But inside the University of South Florida’s newly expanded College of Nursing, Sawyer and her classmates now have a place to make mistakes before the consequences become real. “This simulation center gives us a safe place to make those mistakes, where we can build confidence and grow before someone’s health or life depends on the decisions that we make,” Sawyer said. “That is an incredible gift.” USF officials, along with Sawyer and others, marked the opening of the 42,000-square-foot expansion to the College of Nursing building on the university’s Tampa campus Friday with a ribbon-cutting ceremony. The $33 million project adds classrooms, learning labs and realistic clinical environments intended to help USF train hundreds more nurses as Florida contends with a persistent shortage. The expansion includes the College of Nursing-Tampa General Hospital Nursing Simulation Center, funded through a $4.4 million investment from Tampa General. It features 12 clinical examination rooms, four learning labs and six high-fidelity simulation rooms with adjoining spaces where students and instructors can review their performance. The rooms can recreate conditions in hospitals, clinics, community settings and long-term care facilities. Students can practice administering medication, assessing patients, identifying sepsis, recognizing a patient’s deteriorating condition and communicating with patients and their families. “This morning is not about a building; it’s about the people,” USF President Moez Limayem told the crowd. “As Florida grows, our communities desperately need more highly qualified nurses.” USF plans to expand undergraduate nursing enrollment by 500 students by 2028. College of Nursing Dean Usha Menon said undergraduate enrollment has already grown by 12%, with nearly 2,000 students pursuing nursing degrees across the college’s programs. Officials from the University of South Florida celebrate the opening of a new expansion to the College of Nursing building on the university’s Tampa campus on Friday, August 14, 2026. Photo by Anastasia Dawson The university graduated a record 247 prelicensure undergraduate nurses in spring 2025, a nearly 45% increase from 2023. More than 96% of USF’s new nursing graduates passed the NCLEX licensing examination on their first attempt, Limayem said. Levels of care Still, Menon said Florida is projected to face a shortage of nearly 20,000 registered nurses over the next decade as the state’s population grows and ages. “Meeting that challenge requires more than just recognizing the need,” Menon said. “It requires investing in the people who will answer the call.” The expansion was made possible by $33 million in state funding approved in 2022. Wilton Simpson, then president of the Florida Senate and now the state’s agriculture commissioner, helped secure the money as lawmakers sought to expand Florida’s healthcare workforce. Simpson’s daughter, USF trustee Lauren Monbarren, said the investment was always intended to accomplish more than adding bricks and mortar to the campus. “It was an investment in the nurses who would one day walk through these doors and go on to care for Floridians in hospitals, clinics, nursing homes, veterans’ facilities and communities across the state,” Monbarren said. Although hospitals have made progress filling nursing positions, staffing challenges continue. Emergency department nurses have a turnover rate of about 20%, while nearly 80% of certified nursing assistants and licensed practical nurses leave their positions within two years, according to the Florida Hospital Association. Large investment For Tampa General, meanwhile, investing in USF’s nursing program is a way to strengthen the pipeline of workers entering hospitals across the region and state. “It’s the single best investment TGH makes every year,” Tampa General president and CEO John Couris said of the hospital’s partnership with USF. “It’s not just about the amount of students we graduate; it’s the quality of students that we graduate.” Tampa General president and CEO John Couris (left) talks with USF President Moez Limayem (right) in a simulation lab inside the newly expanded College of Nursing. Photo by Anastasia Dawson The project also gives students more places to study, collaborate and decompress after exams, Sawyer said. A third-year upper-division nursing student and president of the College of Nursing Student Council, she plans to earn a master’s degree and eventually become a nurse practitioner. Sawyer said she was drawn to nursing by her love of science and a desire to serve others, fostered by childhood volunteer work with her mother at Metropolitan Ministries and a local foster care center. But nursing school has also shown her the weight of the profession. “Nursing is hard,” Sawyer said. “It is a physically and emotionally draining career at times. And while we may not say it out loud all the time, it can be a bit intimidating because we’re all afraid of making a mistake.” The new center is designed to confront that fear with repetition. Students can respond to simulated emergencies, make decisions as a team and review what went wrong without putting a patient at risk. “We don’t train them until they get it right,” Limayem says. “We train them until they no longer get it wrong.” With construction complete, Menon said the building will soon fill with students and faculty. Its effect, however, is meant to extend far beyond USF’s campus. “Every student who walks through these doors," she said, "every discovery made here, every patient whose life is improved because of the education that happens here — those are the legacies that you are helping us build."

results.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved Will Look Way Better Soon
results.description: Halo: Campaign Evolved is set to receive its first major patch next week, one that will give players more control over the game's visuals as well as make improvements to Jackals and Sgt. Johnson. As outlined by the Halo Support X account , a patch coming sometime next week will fix a few pain points for players of Halo Studios' remake. The update should make graphics purists happy, as it will add the ability to disable the game's very noticeable film grain and chromatic aberration. The patch will also include "additional stability improvements across multiple platforms." On the gameplay front, Jackals are receiving some changes so that they can be staggered more reliably when targeting their hands and feet, as has always been the case in Halo. Sgt Johnson is being updated so that he no longer blocks mission progress. This sounds like it will mostly affect the three new prequel missions included as part of the remake, where Johnson occasionally needs to hack open doors before Master Chief can proceed. Marines and Flood Marines will also correctly fire their Assault Rifles with the Magnified Skull turned on. https://twitter.com/HaloSupport/status/2087947309334012346?s=20 It remains to be seen if the patch will address other issues players have spotted since release, including unresponsive enemy AI and cutscenes that lock up and fail to play properly. Halo Studios states there will be more details in the full patch notes when the update is released. It's also worth noting that any mid-mission saved progress will be lost upon downloading the new update, though unlocked missions and rally points will remain. The launch of Halo: Campaign Evolved may not have gone as well as Halo Studios would have liked, with reports indicating the game is off to a slow start on PlayStation 5 and has sold a combined total of 1.2 million copies across all platforms so far. According to one analyst, Halo: Campaign Evolved's greatest competition, particularly on PC, might be Halo itself . The franchise's compilation package, Halo: The Master Chief Collection, released over a decade ago and contains almost the entirety of the Halo franchise, including online multiplayer, and can be bought for $40 at the high end or much cheaper when on sale. When compared to Halo: Campaign Evolved, which only features the first game's campaign, no multiplayer, and retails for $50, it's not hard to see why some players decided this was a fight that didn't need finishing. Given the remake's performance, it's unclear what is coming next for the franchise, though Halo: Campaign Evolved does seemingly tease a Halo 2 remake .
